seo.title: About Stephanie Onuaja
seo.description: Stephanie Onuaja is the textile artist behind Nuaj Studio. Trained in architecture, she cuts, composes and stitches lace, aso-oke and beads into handmade textile art and commissions.

hero.role: Textile artist & founder of Nuaj Studio
hero.intro: I'm a textile artist with a background in architecture. I cut, compose and stitch lace, aso-oke and beads into pieces that hold a story — made by hand, for the places and people they belong to.

portrait.alt: Stephanie Onuaja's silhouette — the Nuaj portrait mark — filled with cobalt lace and mint leaves

story.label: Story
story.question: How did cloth become the work?
title: From buildings
to cloth
paragraphs: I trained and worked in architecture. Like a building, clothing is a basic human need — it protects us and it shapes how we live. Fashion and architecture share the same principles: form and function, structure and materiality.

Fashion has always been a source of inspiration for me, and an avenue for self-expression — an extension of my personality and a representation of my story. Through trial and error, I designed and sewed clothing for myself and for friends, experimenting with colour and patterns reminiscent of my origins.
Nuaj grew from that: a studio where cloth that already carries meaning is cut, composed and stitched into something new.
story.quote: Fashion is self-expression. It is who I am, how I feel, and who I want to be.
story.imageAlt: Collage from Stephanie's sketchbook: a dress she designed and sewed from African-print fabrics

items.title: Architecture
items.text: Form, structure and materiality. A piece is planned the way a building is: on a grid, layer by layer, until it holds together.
items.alt: Hands arranging lace strips and leaves into a composition

items.title: Heritage
items.text: Aso-oke, lace and prints reminiscent of my origins — cloth that already carries celebration and memory.

items.title: Music, dance & words
items.text: Music transcends language, time and place. When I sing, dance or write, I'm drawn back to my centre — and that rhythm ends up in the cloth.
